Hi Alex,

Thanks again for taking the time earlier today — appreciated the clear context on FinSight's batch scoring workload and the 99th percentile latency targets. Quick recap and suggested next steps based on our discussion:

Recap of requirements
- Throughput: ~120 qps during trading hours, with predictable bursts up to ~250 qps for market-open spikes
- Latency SLO: 95% < 150ms; 99% target around 300ms
- Data controls: customer PII in payloads; must meet internal audit requirements
- Availability: need graceful degradation strategy if capacity is constrained

Key risks you raised
- Noisy neighbor effects on shared pools causing 99th percentile spikes
- Wanting clear isolation boundaries and transparent SLOs

Our high-level recommendation
- Given your 99th percentile sensitivity and burst profile, Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) is the most straightforward fit for predictable SLOs and strong isolation.
- Hosted (shared) API can work if you adopt aggressive prefix/KV caching and opt for dedicated routing for critical routes, but it adds variability at the 99th percentile.
- Private VPC/on-prem is available if you need customer-managed networking + KMS, but it has longer onboarding and ops cadence.

Attachments: I attached a short SLA summary and a one-page deployment-options worksheet that maps your requirements to the three modes.

Suggested next steps
1) I can put together a quick cost/latency sketch comparing a small Dedicated pool vs tuned Hosted baseline for your workload (need sample token distribution and a 1-hour qps histogram if available).
2) If you want, we can schedule a technical deep-dive with Marissa (runtime lead) to discuss batching/quantization tradeoffs and how we mitigate noisy neighbors.
3) If Dedicated looks right, we can draft a mutual action plan + timeline for Reserved capacity procurement.

When's a good time next week for a 30-minute follow-up?

Best,
Priyom

Alex / Lindsey — thanks for the questions. Answers below and proposed follow-up items.

Noisy neighbor / Hosted variability
- For our Hosted shared pools, the median customer sees stable 95th/99th latencies within SLAs for typical web workloads. However, for bursty, high-concurrency scoring patterns (like yours), the variance at the 99th can increase. In practice, enterprise customers with strict 99th targets move to Dedicated because it provides capacity reservation and stronger isolation.
- Concrete numbers: on Hosted shared pools we observe occasional 99th spikes in the 1-2% of high-burst windows; magnitude depends on burst size and sequence lengths. We can run a one-week replay on our testbed with your qps histogram to quantify this precisely.

Dedicated capacity scaling & burst options
- Dedicated pools are provisioned with reserved vGPU units. Typical scale-up (adding an extra node) can be done in ~15-30 minutes automated, and we offer short-term burst blocks (on a pre-approved billing profile) that can be applied in minutes for extreme events.
- For strict market-open spikes we recommend a hybrid approach: reserved baseline + a small burst buffer and autoscaling policy with pre-warmed instances for sub-60s scale.

Isolation / security evidence
- We'll share a concise technical note outlining isolation boundaries (namespace separation, KV cache scoping, process/container boundaries) and our audit logs. I'll attach it to the HubSpot security packet for your team.

Proposed next steps (concrete)
- You: share a 1-hour qps histogram + example token-length distribution (redacted) and the top 10 latency-sensitive endpoints.
- Us: run a quick replay on our testbed and deliver a short report with observed 95/99 latencies for Hosted baseline vs a small Dedicated pool; include recommended Dedicated sizing.
- Follow-up call: 30 minutes with Marissa (runtime) — I propose Tue Aug 25, 09:00 PT / 12:00 ET. Does that work?

I'll also upload the isolation note to the Drive link in HubSpot.
